tur42-0: What is tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis), how is it recognised, how long does it last, and should you have a cortisone injection? A comparison of the US and UK guidelines, a short history, six home exercises and warning signs.
tur42-1: Pain on the outer side of the elbow that gets worse with gripping and lifting the wrist. Despite its name, most patients do not play tennis: it arises from overloading the shared tendon of the muscles that extend the wrist. Gradual strengthening exercises are the cornerstone of treatment; most people improve clearly within a year, but the process takes patience.
tur42-3: Yearly incidence in a population study in the USA (2000–2012)
tur42-5: Prevalence among people in jobs with heavy use of the hand and wrist
tur42-6: Recurrence within 1 year after a cortisone injection; 12% after a placebo injection (a single study of 165 patients)
tur42-7: The muscles that extend the wrist and fingers backwards attach by a shared tendon to the bony bump on the outer side of the elbow (the lateral epicondyle). Loading this tendon more than it can handle, or in a way it is not used to, causes pain. The problem is thought to be wear in the tendon and difficulty adapting to load rather than inflammation; this is why the name "lateral elbow tendinopathy" is also used.
tur42-8: The diagnosis is made from your history and an examination; both guidelines rely on this.
tur42-9: Pain on the outer side of the elbow when lifting the wrist against resistance (Cozen's test) or lifting the middle finger against resistance (Maudsley's test) supports the diagnosis. The evidence behind these tests is weak; the findings are considered together.
tur42-10: Usually not needed. BESS recommends considering imaging only when the diagnosis is uncertain. An X-ray is requested mainly in long-lasting cases that do not respond to treatment, to rule out other causes; ultrasound or MRI can be used if needed.
tur42-11: Compression of a nerve in the forearm (the radial nerve), pain referred from the neck and problems in the elbow joint itself can cause similar pain. If there is numbness or tingling in the hand, these causes are assessed separately.
tur42-12: Tennis elbow usually improves with time, but this can take months. According to data reported by BESS, 89% of patients have an overall improvement within the first year, and improvement is faster in the first months. On the other hand, the US physiotherapy guideline states that more than half of people seen in primary care (by a family doctor) may still have some symptoms after 1 year, and that symptoms not fully settling or coming back is seen in 20–38% at 6–12 months.
tur42-13: In other words, "improving" and "going away completely" are not the same: most people get clearly better, while some may have mild symptoms for a long time. Keeping up a gradually progressed exercise programme is the cornerstone of managing this process.
tur42-14: In other words, the short-term relief from the injection can slow recovery in the long term and make the pain more likely to return. If an injection is being considered, this risk should be weighed together with your physician. The 2023 care pathway of the British Elbow and Shoulder Society (BESS) strongly recommends against cortisone injections for tennis elbow.
tur42-16: The name of the condition appeared at the end of the 19th century, when lawn tennis was becoming popular. Research over the last 25 years has shown that treatments giving fast short-term relief are not always the best in the long term.
tur42-17: Henry Morris, a surgeon at the Middlesex Hospital, mentioned this condition as "the lawn tennis arm" in a Lancet article that dealt mostly with riding injuries.
tur42-18: A reader's letter to the British Medical Journal used the heading "Lawn-Tennis Elbow". About two weeks later Henry Morris replied, pointing readers to the article he had published in The Lancet the previous year.
tur42-19: In a study of 185 patients seen by family doctors, cortisone injections gave the fastest result at 6 weeks (92% success); but at 52 weeks success was 91% with physiotherapy, 83% with wait-and-see and 69% with injections. Symptoms often came back after the injection.
tur42-20: In a study of 198 people, most of those who had physiotherapy and most of those who waited and watched had recovered by 1 year; of the 65 people who improved within 6 weeks after a cortisone injection, symptoms later came back in 47.
tur42-21: In a placebo-controlled study of 165 patients in Australia, the proportion fully recovered or much improved at 1 year was 83% in the cortisone group and 96% in the placebo injection group; recurrence was 54% with cortisone and 12% with placebo.
tur42-22: In the study comparing surgery with sham (placebo) surgery, which according to BESS is the only one of its kind, both groups improved by 6 months with no difference between them. The study was stopped early; each group had only 13 patients.
tur42-23: A meta-analysis of 30 studies and 2,123 people suggested that exercise is better than passive treatments, but that the difference is small and the certainty of the evidence low or very low.
tur42-24: The American Physical Therapy Association (APTA) guideline (JOSPT) was published: resistance exercises for the wrist-extending muscles, elbow mobilisation, rigid taping and dry needling were recommended at grade B.
tur42-25: The patient care pathway of the British Elbow and Shoulder Society (BESS) was published: physiotherapy is strongly recommended; cortisone injections and shockwave therapy are strongly recommended against.
tur42-26: The 2022 American Physical Therapy Association (APTA) guideline puts gradual strengthening exercises at the centre of treatment; the British Elbow and Shoulder Society (BESS) also strongly recommends physiotherapy.
tur42-27: Resistance exercises for the wrist-extending muscles are recommended: isometric (the muscle works without changing length), concentric (shortening) or eccentric (lengthening) (B). The load is increased step by step, at a pace the tendon can adapt to.
tur42-28: Mobilisation of the elbow joint is recommended to reduce pain and increase pain-free grip strength in the short term (B); techniques for the neck, upper back and wrist can be added as support if these areas are stiff (C).
tur42-29: It is recommended at grade B in the US physiotherapy guideline to reduce pain and loss of function; BESS, however, states that there is no evidence it is better than placebo, so it cannot currently be recommended. In Türkiye only authorised physicians may perform it.
tur42-30: During periods when the pain flares easily, rigid taping can reduce pain in the short term (B). A forearm strap or wrist support can ease pain immediately when worn during activity (expert opinion); studies on its medium- and long-term effect are conflicting.
tur42-31: If weakness is found on examination, exercises strengthening the shoulder and shoulder blade muscles may be added to the programme (C).
tur42-32: Adjusting gripping, lifting and wrist use at work and in daily life may ease symptoms (E, theoretical evidence).
tur42-33: According to BESS, it may be considered in a small number of people who have not improved despite 3–6 months of non-surgical treatment; however, there is no evidence that it is better than sham surgery.
tur42-34: The American Physical Therapy Association (APTA) guideline (JOSPT, 2022) and the patient care pathway of the British Elbow and Shoulder Society (BESS, 2023), side by side. The letters in brackets are the recommendation grades in the JOSPT guideline (A strong, B moderate, C weak, D conflicting evidence, E theoretical evidence, F expert opinion); BESS divides its recommendations into "strong" and "conditional". The JOSPT guideline does not cover drug and injection treatments (cortisone, PRP) or surgery, and does not include shockwave therapy; treatment is chosen for each person.
tur42-36: In long-lasting pain, isometric, concentric or eccentric resistance exercises for the wrist-extending muscles (B); shoulder and shoulder blade exercises if there is weakness (C).
tur42-37: Physiotherapy should be offered (strong); in primary care, exercise sheets for stretching and eccentric loading.
tur42-38: Elbow mobilisation for short-term pain and pain-free grip strength (B); neck, upper back and wrist if stiff (C); soft tissue mobilisation (C).
tur42-40: Rigid taping in the short term during periods when the pain flares easily (B); a strap or wrist support during activity for immediate relief (expert opinion); conflicting evidence in the medium and long term (D).
tur42-41: An orthosis may be offered, but patients should be told it may not help (conditional).
tur42-43: May reduce pain in the short term; worse results and more frequent recurrence at 1 year (placebo-controlled study of 165 patients).
tur42-45: Patients should be told that PRP (platelet-rich plasma prepared from the person's own blood) may have no benefit over placebo (conditional); injection of the person's own blood should not be used (conditional).
tur42-47: Shockwave therapy should not be used (strong).
tur42-48: Laser for pain and grip strength at follow-up from 4 weeks to 6 months (C); TENS for short-term pain (C); ultrasound therapy on its own, conflicting (D); delivering cortisone or painkilling gel through the skin with ultrasound (phonophoresis) not recommended (C).
tur42-49: Dry needling of the tendon or trigger points (B).
tur42-50: No evidence it is better than placebo; cannot currently be recommended (conditional).
tur42-52: Surgery may be considered in people who have not improved despite 3–6 months of non-surgical treatment; patients should be told there is no evidence it is better than sham surgery (conditional). According to the pathway, referral to a specialist is made if there is no improvement within 12–24 weeks in primary care.
tur42-53: Mild, tolerable pain during exercise is possible; if the pain returns to its starting level by the next day, carry on. Stop if you have sharp or steadily increasing pain, or numbness in the hand. Start with the isometric exercise and move on to the eccentric exercise as the pain eases.
tur42-54: Rest your forearm on a table with your palm facing down and your hand over the edge of the table. Try to lift your wrist while pressing down on the back of your hand with your other hand; the hand should not move. Hold with a force that does not clearly increase pain; the muscle works without changing length (isometric). It is usually well tolerated even during painful periods.
tur42-55: Rest your forearm on a table with your palm facing down. Hold a light weight, such as a full half-litre water bottle. Lift your wrist up with help from your other hand, then let go of the help and lower the weight slowly over 3–4 seconds; the muscle works while lengthening (eccentric). Increase the weight as it gets easier.
tur42-56: Hold your arm out in front of you with the elbow straight and palm facing down. With your other hand, hold the back of your hand and gently bend your wrist down and towards you; feel a stretch on the outer side of your forearm, without clearly increasing pain.
tur42-57: Carry heavy bags on your shoulder or as a backpack rather than in your hand.

More than half of people seen in primary care (by a family doctor) may still have symptoms after 1 year, and symptoms not fully settling or coming back at 6–12 months is reported in 20–38%. Keeping up a gradually progressed exercise programme is the cornerstone of managing this process. According to BESS, surgery may be considered in people who have not improved despite 3–6 months of non-surgical treatment; however, there is no evidence that surgery is better than sham surgery. In the only study reviewed by BESS that compared it with sham surgery, each group had 13 patients and no difference was found between them. So the decision about surgery should be made after an open discussion of expectations.
tur42-62: No. Temporarily cut down on gripping and lifting tasks that clearly increase pain, but do not put the arm in a sling. The tendon gets stronger by adapting to gradually increasing load; based on expert opinion, the US guideline also recommends gradually building load back up, especially for people who use their arm heavily.

tur42-64: Redness, swelling or warmth in the elbow; especially with a fever, it should be assessed the same day, in the emergency department if needed (it may be an infection of the joint or bursa)
tur42-65: If arm pain comes with chest pain, shortness of breath or sweating, call 112 immediately
tur42-66: Elbow pain in a child or teenager
tur42-67: A lump you can feel at the elbow, or pain and swelling in more than one joint

tur42-70: What is heel spur syndrome (plantar fasciitis), how is it recognised, how long does it last, and is the "spur" on an X-ray the cause of the pain? A comparison of the US guideline and the BJSM guide, a short history, six home exercises and warning signs.
tur42-71: It shows up as a stabbing pain in the heel with the first steps in the morning. Although it is commonly called a "heel spur", the main source of pain is usually not the bony bump but strain of the connective tissue in the sole of the foot (the plantar fascia). Most patients improve without surgery; however, recovery can take months, and in some people years.
tur42-72: People who improve within 12 months with non-surgical treatment
tur42-73: In non-athletes, plantar fasciitis is clearly more likely with a body mass index above 27 (odds ratio)
tur42-75: The pain is on the inner, lower part of the heel; it is most noticeable with the first steps in the morning and on getting up after sitting for a long time, and it gets worse with long periods of standing.
tur42-76: The diagnosis is mostly made from your history and an examination; imaging is used more to rule out other causes than to make the diagnosis.
tur42-78: Pain on the inner, lower part of the heel that is worst with the first steps after rest, tenderness when pressing where the fascia attaches to the heel, pain brought on by lifting the big toe upwards (windlass test) and limited upward movement of the ankle are among the findings listed in the US physiotherapy guideline.
tur42-79: It is usually considered when non-surgical treatment has not been enough. The first choice is an X-ray taken standing; ultrasound or MRI is requested if needed. On ultrasound, a fascia thicker than 4 millimetres and darker in appearance suggests plantar fasciitis.
tur42-80: Numbness or burning in the sole of the foot suggests nerve compression (tarsal tunnel), and pain when squeezing the heel from both sides suggests a stress fracture. If the symptoms do not fit or do not settle, causes such as rheumatic diseases, thinning of the heel fat pad and a nodule in the fascia are also considered.
tur42-81: According to a review written for primary care physicians, about 80% of patients improve within 12 months with non-surgical treatment. However, in a study of 174 patients diagnosed with ultrasound at a specialist clinic in Denmark and followed for about 9 years on average, the chance of symptoms persisting, counted from their onset, was about 80% at 1 year, 50% at 5 years and 46% at 10 years. Women and people with pain in both heels had a worse course.
tur42-82: These two figures measure different things: the 80% in the review describes improvement in pain, whereas in the Danish study anyone with even the slightest remaining pain was still counted as having the condition. Participants had had symptoms for close to 10 months on average when they came to the clinic, and the authors note that this group represents more severe cases. In other words, pain eases within a year for most people, but it can take years to go away completely in some. A realistic but hopeful outlook and regular exercise are the cornerstone of managing this process.
tur42-83: This is why the aim of treatment is not to "dissolve" the spur or remove it surgically, but to reduce the load on the fascia and strengthen the tissue. The bony bump usually stays on the X-ray even after the pain has gone; so the spur does not need to disappear for you to recover. In the study that followed 174 patients for a long time, whether or not there was a heel spur also did not affect the long-term course.
tur42-84: A short history of heel spur treatment
tur42-85: For a long time, the bony bump and inflammation were seen as the cause of heel pain. Research over the last twenty years has turned attention to loading of the fascia, to stretching and strengthening, and to the fact that the condition can last a long time.
tur42-86: A review proposed that plantar fasciitis is a process involving wear of the tissue rather than inflammation, and used the name "fasciosis".
tur42-87: Plantar fascia-specific stretching was reported to improve outcomes in long-lasting heel pain; this stretch is still one of the core parts of treatment today.
tur42-88: In a study comparing heavy-load strengthening (heel raises with a towel) with stretching, the strengthening group did better at 3 months; at 12 months the two groups were similar.
tur42-89: 174 patients diagnosed with ultrasound at a specialist clinic in Denmark were followed for about 9 years on average: counting anyone with even the slightest remaining pain as still having the condition, the chance of symptoms persisting from their onset was 50% at 5 years and 46% at 10 years. Fascia thickness at the start and the presence of a heel spur did not affect the long-term course.
tur42-90: A best practice guide (BJSM) prepared with 51 randomised trials, 14 experts and the views of 40 patients was published: the core treatment is stretching, taping and individualised education; if this approach is not enough at about 4–6 weeks, shockwave is added, and if improvement is still insufficient at about 12 weeks, custom insoles are added.
tur42-91: The guideline of the Academy of Orthopaedic Physical Therapy of the American Physical Therapy Association (APTA) was updated (JOSPT): manual therapy, stretching, taping and night splints were recommended at the strongest level (A); not adding ultrasound therapy to stretching exercises was also recommended at grade A.
tur42-92: The treatments recommended at the strongest level (A) in the 2023 guideline of the Academy of Orthopaedic Physical Therapy of the American Physical Therapy Association (APTA) are stretching, manual therapy, taping and, for those with consistent first-step pain in the morning, night splints.
tur42-93: Plantar fascia and calf stretches are recommended at the strongest level (A) to reduce pain and improve function in the short and long term.
tur42-94: Manual therapy for the joints and soft tissues of the foot and leg is recommended to reduce stiffness and pain (A).
tur42-95: Dry needling of trigger points in the calf and sole muscles is recommended at grade B in the US physiotherapy guideline. In Türkiye only authorised physicians may perform it.
tur42-96: Elastic or rigid taping, together with other treatments, is recommended to improve pain and function in the short term (A); in studies the benefit was measured over 1–6 weeks. A night splint for 1–3 months is recommended for those with consistent pain on the first steps in the morning (A); however, other sources find the evidence on night splints conflicting.
tur42-97: Off-the-shelf or custom insoles may help in the short term, not on their own but together with other treatments (C). Shoes that support the heel and are well cushioned should be preferred.
tur42-98: For pain that does not improve despite core treatment, shockwave therapy (ESWT) is an option. A cortisone injection can give short-term relief: in a study comparing it with a salt-water (placebo) injection, pain decreased more at 4 weeks, but no long-term benefit was shown. The fascia can tear in about 2.4% of people who have more than one injection. Surgery is considered in a small number of patients who have not responded to any treatment over a long period.
tur42-99: Treatment options: what do the sources say?
tur42-100: The recommendations of the guideline of the Academy of Orthopaedic Physical Therapy of the American Physical Therapy Association (APTA) (JOSPT, 2023) and of a best practice guide (BJSM, 2021) prepared from 51 randomised trials, expert views and patient preferences, side by side. The letters in brackets are the recommendation grades in the JOSPT guideline (A strong, B moderate, C weak, D conflicting, E theoretical evidence). The BJSM guide arranges treatment in steps; treatment is chosen for each person.
tur42-101: Fascia and calf stretches in the short and long term (A).
tur42-103: Fascia stretching, a core treatment for everyone.
tur42-105: Rigid or elastic tape, together with other treatments, in the short term (A).
tur42-108: Individualised education is a core treatment: load management, explaining the pain, footwear advice, and any accompanying diabetes or excess weight. Comfortable, supportive shoes with the heel slightly higher than the forefoot; avoiding walking barefoot and in flat, unsupportive shoes until recovered.
tur42-109: Education on exercise to maintain or build muscle mass; referral for nutrition if needed (E, weak or theoretical evidence).
tur42-110: Should not be used on their own for short-term pain; may be used together with other treatments.
tur42-111: Not a core treatment; custom insoles if improvement is insufficient at about 12 weeks. Not everyone should be given the same insole.
tur42-112: For 1–3 months in those with consistent pain on the first step in the morning (A).
tur42-115: Second line if the core treatment is not enough at about 4–6 weeks.
tur42-116: No recommendation made, as it was considered outside the scope of physiotherapy.
tur42-117: Manual therapy, dry needling and devices
tur42-118: Manual therapy (A); dry needling (B); low-level laser for short-term pain; ultrasound therapy should not be added to stretching (A); manual therapy, stretching and insoles may be preferred over electrotherapy (D, conflicting evidence).
tur42-119: In Türkiye only authorised physicians may perform dry needling.
tur42-120: Effectiveness not proven in the studies the guide assessed. May be considered as an experimental option when core treatment, shockwave and insoles have not been enough, preferably within a research study or with structured evaluation.

tur42-122: Mild discomfort during the exercises is possible; if the pain does not clearly increase the next morning, you can carry on. Doing the stretches before the first steps in the morning and after sitting for a long time gives the most benefit.
tur42-123: Sit down and rest your painful foot on your other knee. With one hand, pull your toes back towards your shin; feel a stretch in the sole of your foot, in front of the heel. It is especially helpful before the first steps in the morning and after sitting for a long time.
tur42-124: In the same position, bring your back foot slightly forward and bend your knee. Lower your hips without lifting your heel off the floor; you will feel the stretch in the lower part of the calf, near the Achilles tendon.
tur42-125: Stand on the bottom step and place a rolled-up towel under the toes of your painful foot. Always holding on to the handrail or wall, rise up on one foot over 3 seconds, hold for 2 seconds and lower over 3 seconds; when lowering, bring your heel down to the level of the step. If one foot is too hard, start with both feet. As it gets easier, add load with a backpack.
tur42-126: Sit down and place a tennis ball or a water bottle under your painful foot. Roll your foot back and forth from the heel to the toes. During painful periods, using a bottle chilled in the freezer and wrapped in a thin cloth may bring relief; do not apply cold if you have loss of feeling in your foot or diabetes.
tur42-127: It usually improves, but it takes patience. About 80% of patients improve within 12 months with non-surgical treatment. However, in a study that followed 174 patients diagnosed with ultrasound at a specialist clinic in Denmark for a long time, counting anyone with even the slightest remaining pain as still having the condition, the chance of symptoms persisting from their onset was 50% at 5 years and 46% at 10 years. In other words, pain eases within a year for most people, but it can take years to go away completely in some. Stretching, taping and load management are the core treatments during this process.
tur42-128: Do I need an X-ray or MRI?
tur42-129: Usually not; the diagnosis is made from your history and an examination. According to the US physiotherapy guideline, imaging is usually considered when non-surgical treatment has not been enough; the first choice is an X-ray taken standing, with ultrasound or MRI if needed. On ultrasound, a fascia thicker than 4 millimetres and darker in appearance suggests plantar fasciitis.
tur42-130: It is thought that because the foot rests pointing downwards overnight, the fascia and calf muscles rest in a shortened position and are suddenly stretched with the first steps. Stretching before getting out of bed may reduce this pain; a night splint can also be tried by those with consistent morning pain.
tur42-131: Insoles may help in the short term, not on their own but together with stretching and strengthening exercises. The US physiotherapy guideline states this with weak evidence, at the level of "may be used"; in one review the benefit was seen up to about 12 weeks and was not clear in the long term. The BJSM guide adds custom insoles only if improvement is insufficient at about 12 weeks.
tur42-132: Heel pain is usually harmless. In the following cases, however, seek help without delay.
tur42-134: Redness, swelling and warmth in the heel together with a fever (especially if you have diabetes)
tur42-135: Being unable to put weight on the heel after a fall or blow (it may be a fracture)
tur42-136: A sudden tearing sensation in the sole of the foot, bruising and being unable to put weight on it (it may be a tear of the fascia; especially after a cortisone injection)
tur42-137: If you have diabetes: a wound, colour change or coldness in the foot
tur42-138: Back pain together with weakness in the leg or problems with bladder or bowel control

tur42-141: Ankle sprain: its grades, should you walk on a sprained ankle, do you need an X-ray, how long does it last, and why does it recur? A comparison of two guidelines, a short history, six home exercises and warning signs.
tur42-142: The ankle usually rolls inwards, straining or tearing the ligaments on the outer side. Most sprains heal without surgery. Early, gradual weight-bearing and exercise support recovery; balance exercises and an ankle brace reduce the risk of the same ankle being sprained again.
tur42-143: If you cannot take them both right after the injury and at the examination, an X-ray is needed (Ottawa rules)
tur42-144: People who developed chronic instability at 12 months in a study following people after their first sprain
tur42-146: When the ankle twists inwards suddenly and forcefully, the ligaments in front of and below the outer ankle bone (malleolus) are stretched or torn. There is pain, swelling and bruising, and putting weight on the foot becomes difficult.
tur42-147: Support the ankle with tape or an ankle brace, and put weight on it as far as the pain allows.
tur42-148: Intermittent ice and raising the leg may help reduce swelling.
tur42-150: Sprains are divided into three grades according to the damage to the ligament. The grade gives an idea of recovery time and how much support is needed. According to the guidelines, ligament damage is assessed most accurately by an examination 4–5 days after the injury.
tur42-151: Partial, mild damage to the ligament; mild tenderness and swelling. You can put weight on it and walk with little pain; no looseness in the joint.
tur42-152: A more marked but incomplete tear of the ligament; moderate pain and swelling, mild to moderate bruising. Putting weight on it and walking are painful; there may be mild to moderate looseness.
tur42-153: A complete tear of the ligament; marked swelling and bruising, unable to put weight on it or walk, clear looseness of the joint on examination.
tur42-154: Most sprains involve no fracture and do not need an X-ray. The Ottawa ankle rules were developed to identify the patients who do need an X-ray, and in a review combining 27 studies they picked up 97.6% of fractures. Using only part of the rule (for example, only whether you can walk) lowers its accuracy; the whole rule should be applied.
tur42-155: Ankle X-ray: if there is pain in the ankle area together with bony tenderness along the back edge of the lower 6 centimetres of the shin bone or the outer leg bone, or at the tip of the inner or outer ankle bone (malleolus), or if 4 steps cannot be taken (even with a limp) both right after the injury and at the examination. Foot X-ray: if there is pain in the middle of the foot together with tenderness at the base of the 5th metatarsal (the bump on the outer edge of the foot) or the navicular bone (the bump on the inner edge of the foot), or if 4 steps cannot be taken in the same way.
tur42-156: According to data reported in the US physiotherapy guideline, only about half of people who sprain an ankle seek medical care. Return to work or sport can vary from 1 day to a little over 3 weeks depending on the activity. However, the pain going away does not mean the ankle has fully recovered: pain lasts 1 year or longer in 5–33% of people, and full recovery at about 3 years is reported in 50–85%. With severe sprains, recovery can take months.
tur42-157: Chronic instability: In a study that followed people after their first sprain, 40% had developed chronic instability at 12 months, with the ankle repeatedly giving way and spraining, while 60% recovered without problems. Balance and neuromuscular control exercises matter both for recovery and for preventing this.
tur42-158: A short history of sprain treatment
tur42-159: For a long time, rest and immobilisation were at the forefront of sprain care. Research over more than the last twenty years has clarified how to decide on an X-ray and shown the importance of early, gradual movement and balance exercises.
tur42-160: In a review combining 27 studies and 15,581 people, the Ottawa ankle rules picked up 97.6% of fractures; it was concluded that the rules are reliable for identifying patients who do not need an X-ray.
tur42-161: In a study of 584 patients with severe sprains at 8 emergency departments in the United Kingdom, a below-knee cast for 10 days gave faster recovery than a tubular elastic bandage, and an Aircast-type ankle brace gave better function at 3 months. By 9 months there was no difference between the groups. The authors recommended the below-knee cast, which showed the broadest benefit.
tur42-162: In a study of 101 people with mild to moderate sprains, those given an early exercise programme in the first week had better function at weeks 1 and 2 than those given conventional care of protection, rest, ice, compression and elevation.
tur42-163: A study combining 46 systematic reviews found strong evidence for ankle braces and moderate evidence for neuromuscular control (balance) exercises in preventing repeat sprains.
tur42-164: An evidence-based guideline was updated (BJSM): ligament damage is best assessed by an examination 4–5 days after the injury; supervised exercise programmes are preferred over passive treatments; surgery is reserved for those who do not respond to thorough exercise-based treatment.
tur42-165: The guideline of the Academy of Orthopaedic Physical Therapy of the American Physical Therapy Association (APTA) was updated (JOSPT): external support with gradual loading, structured exercise and manual therapy were recommended at the strongest level (A); not using ultrasound therapy was recommended (A).
tur42-166: The 2021 guideline (JOSPT) of the Academy of Orthopaedic Physical Therapy of the American Physical Therapy Association (APTA) groups treatment after a sprain under the following headings.
tur42-167: Protecting the ankle with external support such as tape or an ankle brace and gradually putting weight on the foot are recommended (A). Severe injuries may need immobilisation for up to 10 days.

In the first days, do only this up-and-down movement within a pain-free range; as the pain eases, you can also draw small circles with your ankle without forcing it. It helps reduce swelling and maintain movement.

Keeping your heel on the floor and without moving your knee, turn your foot outwards from the ankle and slowly bring it back. It strengthens the muscles on the outer side of the ankle.

As it gets easier, increase the difficulty one step at a time: first let go of the support, then close your eyes or try on a soft surface such as a folded towel; keep your hand close to the counter while trying these. People with balance problems and older adults should not do these stages without support. It is the key exercise for preventing new sprains.

If you cannot take 4 steps after the injury or there is clear tenderness over the bone, you first need to be assessed for a fracture (see "Do I need an X-ray?"). The American Physical Therapy Association guideline recommends protecting a newly sprained ankle with support such as tape or an ankle brace and gradually putting weight on the foot. Not putting any weight on it for a long time can delay recovery.
tur42-198: Most sprains do not need one. According to the Ottawa rules, an ankle X-ray is needed if there is pain in the ankle area together with bony tenderness along the back edge of the lower 6 centimetres of the shin bone or the outer leg bone, or at the tip of the inner or outer ankle bone (malleolus), or if 4 steps cannot be taken (even with a limp) both right after the injury and at the examination. A foot X-ray is needed if there is pain in the middle of the foot together with tenderness at the base of the 5th metatarsal (the bump on the outer edge of the foot) or the navicular bone (the bump on the inner edge of the foot). These rules pick up almost all fractures.
tur42-199: It depends on the grade of the sprain. According to the US physiotherapy guideline, return to work or sport can range from 1 day to a little over 3 weeks depending on the activity. However, recovery may not be complete even when the pain has gone: in studies, pain lasted 1 year or longer in 5–33% of people, and full recovery at about 3 years was reported in 50–85%. With severe sprains, recovery can take months. This is why it is important to keep up balance and strengthening exercises after the pain has gone.
tur42-200: If a ligament is torn, do I need surgery?
tur42-201: Usually not. Even complete ligament tears are generally treated without surgery: short-term support, gradual loading and an exercise programme. The guideline published in BJSM in 2018 reserves surgery for cases that do not respond to thorough, properly delivered exercise-based treatment.
tur42-202: Intermittent, repeated ice together with an exercise programme is among the methods the guideline lists as usable to reduce pain and swelling. Do not put ice directly on the skin; keep a thin cloth in between. England's National Health Service (NHS) recommends applying it for up to 20 minutes every 2–3 hours.
tur42-203: Should I use an ankle brace?
tur42-204: Using support such as tape or an ankle brace for a new sprain is recommended. For people who have had a sprain, wearing an ankle brace during sport and doing balance exercises are also recommended to prevent new sprains. A study combining 46 systematic reviews found strong evidence for ankle braces and moderate evidence for neuromuscular control (balance) exercises in preventing repeat sprains; for a new sprain, the evidence for early movement was strong.
tur42-205: If balance, muscle strength and the ankle's sense of position have not fully recovered after a sprain, the ankle becomes prone to spraining again. Keeping up balance and strengthening exercises even after the pain has gone and returning to sport gradually help break this cycle. In footballers, the FIFA 11+ warm-up programme done regularly before training reduced the overall injury rate by 39% in a meta-analysis combining 4 studies; these studies were not specific to people who had had a previous sprain.

tur42-220: Most people improve clearly with non-surgical treatment; however, in some people symptoms can last for months or come back. According to the 2025 care pathway of the British Elbow and Shoulder Society (BESS), most symptoms usually respond within 3 months; if there is no improvement by 12 weeks, specialist assessment is recommended. An exercise programme with gradually increasing load is the cornerstone of treatment.
